title: What a Chief Justice Actually Controls
hook: The chief justice's vote counts the same as everyone else's. The real power is procedural — who speaks, who writes, and in what order — and none of it is in the Constitution.
key_points: The Constitution mentions the office but grants it no specific powers beyond presiding over a presidential impeachment trial.
The chief presides over oral argument, running the order in which justices question counsel.
The chief presides over the justices' private conference, framing each case and leading the vote.
When in the majority, the chief assigns who writes the opinion — the most consequential of the three powers.
Law professor Josh Blackman argues these roles should be delegated, noting Justice Stevens presided during Chief Justice Rehnquist's 2004 illness without disruption.
content_html: Ask what makes the chief justice powerful and most people reach for the vote. That is the wrong place to look: the chief holds one vote out of nine, the same as anyone else. The influence lives in procedure — and, unusually for such a visible office, almost none of it is written down in the Constitution.
extra_html: Writing at SCOTUSblog, law professor Josh Blackman inventories three levers. The chief presides over oral argument, controlling the flow of questioning. The chief presides over the justices' private conference, where each case is framed and votes are taken. And when the chief is in the majority, the chief decides who writes the opinion — the lever that matters most, because the assignment shapes how broad or narrow the resulting rule will be. Blackman's argument is that these should be shared: rotating them would let other justices learn the job, encourage procedural experimentation, spread opinion assignments more evenly, and keep a little humility in the center chair. His evidence that the Court can survive it is historical — when Chief Justice Rehnquist fell ill in 2004 and after his death, Justice Stevens presided over arguments and conference, and the institution kept working. Whether or not you find the proposal persuasive, it clarifies a useful civics point: much of what looks like constitutional structure is actually internal custom, and custom can be rearranged.

related.title: How the Supreme Court Decides a Case
related.hook: A top court hears only a sliver of the cases that beg for its attention — and the path from petition to ruling runs through written briefs, a public argument, and a vote taken in secret.

related.title: Nine Justices, Nine Styles
related.hook: One scholar coded 5,095 questions from a full Supreme Court term and found each justice interrogates lawyers in a signature way — a fingerprint of how they think about the law.

related.title: Not All Dissents Are Created Equal
related.hook: Dissent tallies treat a one-line 'I would deny' the same as a fully reasoned opinion. One scholar sorted 386 of them on the emergency docket — and found about half were just bare votes.

related.title: What a Concurrence Is For
related.hook: A concurring justice agrees with the outcome — and sometimes uses the space to propose demolishing the doctrine the majority just applied. Today's lone concurrence is tomorrow's majority.

flashcards.prompt: Which power gives a chief justice the most influence over the law?

choices.text: Assigning who writes the majority opinion when the chief is in the majority
Casting two votes in close cases
Vetoing a case the other justices want to hear

flashcards.explanation_html: The vote is one of nine, but the assignment decides whose reasoning becomes the binding statement of the law.

flashcards.prompt: Where do the chief justice's day-to-day powers come from?
flashcards.back_html: Mostly from custom and internal practice, not the Constitution — which names the office but grants it almost no specific authority.

flashcards.prompt: What historical example does Blackman use to argue the role can be shared?

choices.text: Justice Stevens presided over argument and conference during Rehnquist's 2004 illness
The Court operated with no chief justice for a decade
Congress once split the chief justiceship between two people

flashcards.explanation_html: The Court kept functioning with the senior associate justice in the chair — evidence, he says, that delegation is workable.
